extracted.intended_audience: scholars and policymakers in public administration, AI governance, and survey research
extracted.subtask_short: survey measures for public opinion on AI
extracted.subtask_description: Defines survey constructs, measurement items, and validity/analysis standards used to assess public trust, perceived risk, and policy preferences for AI regulation in a nationally representative US survey. Useful for designing, evaluating, or interpreting public-opinion research on AI governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for slowing AI development (DV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct: 'support for slowing down AI development' — the average of three items: 'I support public campaigns to slow down AI development,' 'I support government regulation that slows down AI development,' and 'I oppose government regulation that slows down AI development' (the opposition item reverse coded). Each item measured on 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree) Likert-type scales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composite formed by averaging the three items (reverse-code opposition item first). Used as one dependent variable representing softer regulatory preferences. Cronbach's alpha and factor checks reported for composites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for banning advanced AI technologies (DV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct: 'support for banning the development of advanced AI technologies' — the average of three items: 'I support banning the development of artificial general intelligence that is smarter than humans,' 'I support a global ban on data centers that are large enough to train AI systems that are smarter than humans,' and 'I support a global ban on the development of sentience in robots/AIs.' Items measured on 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree) Likert-type scales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composite formed by averaging the three items. Used as one dependent variable representing stronger regulatory preferences (immediate bans). Items were inspired by Metzinger’s moratorium proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust in government (IV / institutional trust)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured as the average of three items intended as proxies for governmental competency to manage and regulate AI: (1) 'AI systems include many different parts. To what extent do you trust the following parts…governments?' (1 not at all to 7 very much sliding scale), (2) 'To what extent do you agree or disagree that governments have the power to effectively enforce regulations on the development of AI?' (1 strongly disagree to 7 strongly agree), and (3) 'Do you think that governments have the power to regulate the development of AI?' (categorical transformed: no=1, not sure=4, yes=7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct rationale: focuses on perceived competency (capability/effectiveness). Authors also report robustness checks using both the three-item index and a single-item measure (the first item) to address validity concerns that some items may measure regulatory competency rather than generalized trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust in AI industry / companies (IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured as the average of three items assessing trust, benevolence, and competency of AI creators: (1) 'AI systems include many different parts. To what extent do you trust the following parts…companies?' (1 not at all to 7 very much sliding scale), (2) 'Do you trust that the creators of large language models (e.g., OpenAI and GPT-4) put safety over profits?' and (3) 'Do you trust that the creators of an AI can control all current and future versions of the AI?' (the latter two measured categorically and transformed: no=1, not sure=4, yes=7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index captures institutional trust in private developers; used to test hypotheses that industry trust decreases support for regulation. Composite averaging and transformations applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust in AI technologies (IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured as the average of four items with the stem 'I trust' paired with: 'chatbots,' 'large language models,' 'robots,' and 'game-playing AI.' Each item measured on 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree) Likert-type scales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captures perceptual trust in AI systems themselves (distinct from institutional trust). Used to test whether trust in technologies predicts lower support for softer and stronger regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived AI risk (IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured as the average of four items: 'AI is likely to cause human extinction,' 'Robots/AIs may be harmful to me personally,' 'Robots/AIs may be harmful to people in the USA,' and 'Robots/AIs may be harmful to future generations of people.' Items measured on 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree) Likert-type scales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composite represents perceived existential and societal risks from AI. Used to test hypotheses that higher perceived risk increases support for both softer and stronger regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and typology of regulatory strength (soft vs strong)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stronger regulations: immediate full prohibitions or bans (e.g., bans on real-time biometric surveillance; local bans on facial recognition in policing). Softer regulations: government programs aiming to limit some AI applications or slow down technology development without direct enforcement, intervention in development pace via non-mandatory means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors locate policy tools along a continuum of severity; empirical dependent variables map to this typology (slowdown = softer; bans = stronger). Examples given from EU AI Act, local U.S. bans, and Japan's softer approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional trust conceptualization (competency, benevolence, integrity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trust is conceptualized to trace causes such as perceived competency and ability, perceived benevolence, and perceived integrity of institutions. For this study, perceived competency (governmental competency to manage/regulate AI) was particularly emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurement choices prioritize competency-related items for government trust; authors cite literature validating multi-dimensional conceptualizations of trust and justify item selection accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling and representativeness standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Data: nationally representative US sample (AIMS 2023 supplement, N = 1,099). Sample recruited according to 2021 ACS estimates for age, education, race/ethnicity, gender, income, and region using leading panels (iSay/Ipsos, Dynata, Disqo, others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodology was preregistered on OSF and the dataset is openly available on Mendeley Data. Use of census-based quotas and reputable panels is the stated standard for achieving national representativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement scale and item transformation practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of multiple item response formats: sliding scales (1–7), Likert-type scales (1–7), categorical items transformed to numeric (no=1, not sure=4, yes=7), exposure-frequency items measured 0 (never) to 5 (daily). Reverse coding applied where appropriate (e.g., opposition item in slowdown support).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors justify combining differently formatted items into composites via transformation and report sensitivity/robustness checks. Explicitly documents transformations for transparency and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite construction and robustness checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Composites formed by averaging multiple items after appropriate coding/transformations (e.g., trust indices, policy preference indices, perceived risk). Authors perform robustness checks, e.g., reporting regression results using both multi-item indices and single-item measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard practice reported: average items into indices, conduct sensitivity analyses using alternative operationalizations to address validity concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychometric and factor-analysis validity criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported validity checks include Cronbach's alpha for internal consistency (most major composite variables have α > 0.6), Kaiser Criterion for factor retention (principal component/factor eigenvalues > 1), and Harman's one-factor test for common method bias (one factor extracted accounts for 37% of variance, below the 50% threshold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors treat α > 0.6 and eigenvalue>1 as evidence of acceptable reliability and content validity. Harman's <50% is used as suggestive evidence that common method bias is less of a concern, though not definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control variable standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses control for gender, political orientation, race/ethnicity, income, education, and frequency of exposure to AI systems and to news or stories about AI (exposure frequency operationalized as the average of two items measured 0–5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion of these sociodemographic and exposure controls is the stated standard to isolate relationships between trust, perceived risk, and regulation preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical reporting and transparency practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors preregistered the AIMS survey methodology on OSF and made data openly available (Mendeley Data). They report descriptive statistics, correlations, Cronbach's alphas, principal component/factor diagnostics, and note use of principal component/factor methods and Harman's test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended/used practices: preregistration, open data, reporting of item-level descriptive stats and psychometric diagnostics, and explicit discussion of common method bias limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical hypotheses linking trust and perceived risk to regulatory preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit hypotheses: Hypothesis 1a/b (Government trust increases support for softer and stronger regulation), Hypothesis 2a/b (AI industry trust decreases support for softer and stronger regulation), Hypothesis 3a/b (Trust in AI technologies decreases support for softer and stronger regulation), Hypothesis 4a/b (Perceived AI risks increase support for softer and stronger regulations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These hypotheses constitute the theoretical evaluation framework used to interpret empirical model estimates and to adjudicate whether trust and risk predict policy preferences.
